summary.text: Introduce auxiliary sequences \(y_0=-2,y_1=-352\) and \(z_0=-56,z_1=-2176\), both satisfying \(u_{k+2}=112u_{k+1}-4096u_k\); algebraic identities coupling \(y\) and \(z\), together with the derived recurrence \(a_{n+6}=-48a_{n+4}+3072a_{n+2}+262144a_n\), allow a simultaneous induction proving \(a_{4k+1}=y_k^2\) and \(a_{4k+3}=z_k^2\). Splitting the index by parity then places every relevant odd-indexed term in one of these two square families.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that every term with odd index is a square. More precisely, we will construct two auxiliary integer sequences \((y_k)\) and \((z_k)\) and prove
\[
a_{4k+1}=y_k^2,\qquad a_{4k+3}=z_k^2
\tag{2}
\]
for every \(k\ge 0\). This immediately covers every index of the form \(2n+1\).

Define the auxiliary sequences by
\[
y_0=-2,\qquad y_1=-352,
\]
\[
z_0=-56,\qquad z_1=-2176,
\]
and give both sequences the same second-order recurrence
\[
y_{k+2}=112y_{k+1}-4096y_k,
\qquad
z_{k+2}=112z_{k+1}-4096z_k
\tag{3}
\]
for \(k\ge 0\).

We first establish the identities between these auxiliary sequences that will make their squares obey the appropriate recurrence.

First, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
z_{k+1}=12y_{k+1}-1024y_k.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, both sides, viewed as sequences in \(k\), obey the recurrence
\[
u_{k+2}=112u_{k+1}-4096u_k.
\]
For the left side this follows directly from the recurrence for \(z\); for the right side it follows because a fixed linear combination of two shifts of a solution of a linear recurrence is again a solution. It therefore suffices to check two consecutive values. From (3),
\[
y_2=112(-352)-4096(-2)=-31232,
\]
and
\[
z_2=112(-2176)-4096(-56)=-14336.
\]
At \(k=0\),
\[
12y_1-1024y_0=12(-352)-1024(-2)=-4224+2048=-2176=z_1.
\]
At \(k=1\),
\[
12y_2-1024y_1=12(-31232)-1024(-352)
=-374784+360448=-14336=z_2.
\]
Thus (4) follows for all \(k\).

Second, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
4y_{k+1}=-z_{k+1}+64z_k.
\tag{5}
\]
Again, both sides satisfy the same second-order recurrence, so two initial checks suffice. For \(k=0\),
\[
4y_1=4(-352)=-1408
\]
and
\[
-z_1+64z_0=2176+64(-56)=2176-3584=-1408.
\]
For \(k=1\), using the values of \(y_2,z_2\) computed above,
\[
4y_2=4(-31232)=-124928,
\]
while
\[
-z_2+64z_1=14336+64(-2176)=14336-139264=-124928.
\]
This proves (5).

Combining (4) and (5) gives a further useful identity. Equation (5) says
\[
z_{k+1}+4y_{k+1}=64z_k.
\]
Substituting (4) into this equality gives
\[
16y_{k+1}-1024y_k=64z_k.
\]
Dividing by \(16\), we obtain
\[
4z_k=y_{k+1}-64y_k.
\tag{6}
\]

We next derive two identities for squares.

Using (4) and (6), set \(u=y_{k+1}\) and \(v=y_k\). Then
\[
z_{k+1}=12u-1024v,
\qquad
4z_k=u-64v.
\]
A direct expansion yields
\[
16z_{k+1}^2
=-768y_{k+1}^2+3072(4z_k)^2+4194304y_k^2.
\tag{7}
\]
For completeness, after the substitution the left side is
\[
16(12u-1024v)^2
=2304u^2-393216uv+16777216v^2.
\]
The right side is
\[
-768u^2+3072(u-64v)^2+4194304v^2,
\]
which expands to
\[
(-768+3072)u^2-393216uv
+(3072\cdot4096+4194304)v^2,
\]
namely the same expression
\[
2304u^2-393216uv+16777216v^2.
\]
Thus (7) is proved.

There is a companion identity for \(y_{k+2}^2\). Applying (5) with index \(k+1\) and then using the recurrence for \(z\), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
4y_{k+2}
&=-z_{k+2}+64z_{k+1}\\
&=-(112z_{k+1}-4096z_k)+64z_{k+1}\\
&=-48z_{k+1}+4096z_k\\
&=-48z_{k+1}+1024(4z_k).
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Also, (5) can be written as
\[
4y_{k+1}=-z_{k+1}+16(4z_k).
\tag{9}
\]
Squaring (8), and using (9), gives
\[
16y_{k+2}^2
=-768z_{k+1}^2+3072(4y_{k+1})^2+262144(4z_k)^2.
\tag{10}
\]
To check this polynomial identity explicitly, put \(p=z_{k+1}\) and \(q=4z_k\). Its left side is
\[
(-48p+1024q)^2
=2304p^2-98304pq+1048576q^2.
\]
Its right side, using \(4y_{k+1}=-p+16q\), is
\[
-768p^2+3072(-p+16q)^2+262144q^2.
\]
This expands to
\[
(-768+3072)p^2-98304pq
+(3072\cdot256+262144)q^2,
\]
which is again
\[
2304p^2-98304pq+1048576q^2.
\]
Hence (10) holds.

We now derive from the original fourth-order recurrence a recurrence involving every second term. We claim that for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+6}=-48a_{n+4}+3072a_{n+2}+262144a_n.
\tag{11}
\]
Starting with (1) at index \(n+2\), and then substituting (1) for \(a_{n+5}\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+6}
&=-4a_{n+5}+256a_{n+3}+4096a_{n+2}\\
&=-4(-4a_{n+4}+256a_{n+2}+4096a_{n+1})
  +256a_{n+3}+4096a_{n+2}\\
&=16a_{n+4}+256a_{n+3}+3072a_{n+2}-16384a_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Meanwhile, (1) at index \(n\) gives
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\]
Multiplying this equality by \(-64\) and rearranging yields
\[
256a_{n+3}-16384a_{n+1}=-64a_{n+4}+262144a_n.
\]
Substituting this in the preceding expression for \(a_{n+6}\) proves (11).

We are now ready to prove (2). Because the induction step advances \(k\) by two, we first verify the cases \(k=0\) and \(k=1\).

For \(k=0\), the defining initial values give
\[
a_1=4=(-2)^2=y_0^2,
\qquad
a_3=3136=(-56)^2=z_0^2.
\]

For \(k=1\), we calculate the required later terms from (1). First,
\[
a_4=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)=-15616.
\]
Then
\[
a_5=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1
=62464+45056+16384=123904=(-352)^2=y_1^2.
\]
For use in computing \(a_7\),
\[
a_6=-4a_5+256a_3+4096a_2
=-495616+802816+720896=1028096.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_7
&=-4a_6+256a_4+4096a_3\\
&=-4112384-3997696+12845056\\
&=4734976=(-2176)^2=z_1^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (2) holds for \(k=0,1\).

Suppose now that for some \(k\ge 0\), (2) is already known at both \(k\) and \(k+1\); that is,
\[
a_{4k+1}=y_k^2,\qquad a_{4k+3}=z_k^2,
\tag{12}
\]
and
\[
a_{4k+5}=y_{k+1}^2,\qquad a_{4k+7}=z_{k+1}^2.
\tag{13}
\]
We prove it at \(k+2\).

Apply (11) with \(n=4k+3\). Since
\[
n+6=4k+9=4(k+2)+1,
\]
we obtain
\[
a_{4k+9}=-48a_{4k+7}+3072a_{4k+5}+262144a_{4k+3}.
\]
Using (12) and (13), this becomes
\[
a_{4k+9}
=-48z_{k+1}^2+3072y_{k+1}^2+262144z_k^2.
\tag{14}
\]
Now divide identity (10) by \(16\). Because
\[
\frac{3072(4y_{k+1})^2}{16}=3072y_{k+1}^2
\]
and
\[
\frac{262144(4z_k)^2}{16}=262144z_k^2,
\]
that identity says exactly
\[
y_{k+2}^2
=-48z_{k+1}^2+3072y_{k+1}^2+262144z_k^2.
\]
Comparison with (14) gives
\[
a_{4(k+2)+1}=a_{4k+9}=y_{k+2}^2.
\tag{15}
\]

It remains to prove the corresponding assertion at the index \(4(k+2)+3\). Apply (11) with \(n=4k+5\). This gives
\[
a_{4k+11}=-48a_{4k+9}+3072a_{4k+7}+262144a_{4k+5}.
\]
Using (15) and (13),
\[
a_{4k+11}
=-48y_{k+2}^2+3072z_{k+1}^2+262144y_{k+1}^2.
\tag{16}
\]
Apply (7) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\):
\[
16z_{k+2}^2
=-768y_{k+2}^2+3072(4z_{k+1})^2+4194304y_{k+1}^2.
\]
Dividing by \(16\), and noting that
\[
\frac{3072(4z_{k+1})^2}{16}=3072z_{k+1}^2,
\qquad
\frac{4194304}{16}=262144,
\]
we get
\[
z_{k+2}^2
=-48y_{k+2}^2+3072z_{k+1}^2+262144y_{k+1}^2.
\]
Together with (16), this proves
\[
a_{4(k+2)+3}=a_{4k+11}=z_{k+2}^2.
\]
Thus the truth of (2) at \(k\) and \(k+1\) implies its truth at \(k+2\). Since it holds at \(0\) and \(1\), two-step induction proves (2) for every nonnegative integer \(k\).

Finally, let \(n\ge 0\). If \(n\) is even, write \(n=2k\). Then
\[
2n+1=4k+1,
\]
so (2) gives
\[
a_{2n+1}=a_{4k+1}=y_k^2.
\]
If \(n\) is odd, write \(n=2k+1\). Then
\[
2n+1=4k+3,
\]
and (2) gives
\[
a_{2n+1}=a_{4k+3}=z_k^2.
\]
In either case \(a_{2n+1}\) is the square of an integer. Therefore, for every nonnegative integer \(n\), \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square.
